abstract: Stellate ganglion block (SGB) improves sleep in clinical populations, yet the mechanisms linking sympathetic activity to human microglial states remain untested. A prerequisite is to establish what sympathetic signaling readouts exist in human microglia and whether state composition changes in a disease-relevant physiological dimension. Using two public human single-nucleus datasets (the ROSMAP prefrontal cortex resource: 443 donors, 174,420 immune nuclei, 152,459 microglial nuclei, 12 published microglial states; and a hippocampal multiome cohort spanning adult lifespan: 40 donors, ages 20 - 100, 15,225 microglial nuclei), we quantified (i) adrenergic receptor and inflammatory/complement axis gene expression across microglial states, and (ii) donor-level trajectories of four microglial state signatures across age. Adrenergic receptors were barely detected: among nine receptor genes, only ADRB2 was detectable in 3.8 - 11.4% of nuclei, and no adrenergic receptor was state-specific. In contrast, inflammatory genes (nuclear factor-{kappa}B and interleukin modules) were strongly concentrated in one pro-inflammatory state (e.g., NFKB1 mean expression 1.47 vs 0.35 - 0.72 in other states; IL1B in 32.6% of nuclei vs 2 - 16% elsewhere), complement genes in a complement-enriched state, and lipid-metabolism/disease-associated genes in a distinct state. Across the adult lifespan, hippocampal microglia showed a donor-level decline of the homeostatic signature (mean score 0.70 to 0.38 across age quartiles; Spearman {rho} = -0.55, P = 2.6 * 10-4), with concordant rises of pro-inflammatory ({rho} = 0.37, P = 0.017) and disease-associated/lipid-metabolism ({rho} = 0.32, P = 0.045) signatures; an interferon signature showed no age trend. These results (a) indicate that human microglia lack a robust direct adrenergic receptor substrate at single-nucleus resolution, implying that sympathetic influence on microglia, if causal, is likely indirect or low-frequency, and (b) establish a donor-level, age-associated baseline shift toward inflammatory/trimming states in the human hippocampus. Together they define candidate readouts and the baseline against which chronic-sleep-disorder and neuromodulation-intervention studies (e.g., SGB) should be designed.
